raw_text:
Sacubitril/valsartan is the prototype angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI) and represents one of the most important advances in pharmacologic heart-failure therapy. Its biologic rationale is dual: blockade of the renin-angiotensin system through valsartan, and augmentation of endogenous natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, adrenomedullin, and related vasoactive peptides through neprilysin inhibition [1]. Early pharmacodynamic studies showed that LCZ696, later named sacubitril/valsartan, increased cyclic guanosine monophosphate and natriuretic peptide activity while providing angiotensin II receptor blockade [2]. The concept followed earlier experience with vasopeptidase inhibition: omapatrilat improved some hemodynamic and clinical measures but was limited by excess angioedema, attributed to simultaneous ACE and neprilysin inhibition [3], [4]. Pairing neprilysin inhibition with an angiotensin receptor blocker rather than an ACE inhibitor was therefore central to the development of sacubitril/valsartan. Dose-finding in hypertension and phase 2 heart-failure studies established biologic activity, blood-pressure lowering, and favorable biomarker changes [5], [6].

The pivotal evidence in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) came from PARADIGM-HF, designed to compare sacubitril/valsartan 97/103 mg twice daily with enalapril 10 mg twice daily after sequential run-in periods [7]. The trial was stopped early because sacubitril/valsartan reduced the primary composite of cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalization, as well as all-cause mortality [8]. Subsequent analyses showed that benefit was not confined to the first event: sacubitril/valsartan reduced clinical progression, recurrent hospitalization, and intensification of therapy [9]. It also lowered both sudden death and death from worsening heart failure, consistent with broad disease-modifying effects rather than merely decongestion [10].

The HFrEF benefit appears clinically robust across major subgroups. Relative efficacy was preserved in older patients, although hypotension and renal dysfunction require closer monitoring in frailty and multimorbidity [11]. Baseline systolic blood pressure modifies tolerability but not the direction of benefit, supporting cautious initiation even in lower-pressure patients when clinically stable [12]. Analyses of achieved dose suggest that patients unable to reach target dose may still derive benefit compared with similarly reduced enalapril exposure [13]. Renal analyses found slower decline in estimated glomerular filtration rate compared with enalapril, despite slightly higher albuminuria, and fewer severe renal events in some subgroups [14]. Among patients receiving mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, sacubitril/valsartan was associated with less severe hyperkalemia than enalapril, which may facilitate background guideline-directed therapy [15]. In diabetes, it improved glycemic indices modestly and reduced the need for insulin initiation, possibly through natriuretic peptide–mediated metabolic effects [16]. Changes in NT-proBNP after treatment were strongly prognostic, although BNP interpretation is complicated because BNP is a neprilysin substrate [17].

Patient-centered outcomes also support use. Sacubitril/valsartan improved or slowed deterioration in health-related quality of life compared with enalapril [18], and secondary analyses suggested favorable effects on physical and social activity limitations [19]. Implementation studies then addressed practical initiation. TITRATION showed that both condensed and conservative uptitration strategies were feasible, with slower uptitration useful in patients previously receiving low-dose ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy [20]. In hospitalized acute decompensated HFrEF, PIONEER-HF showed that in-hospital initiation after hemodynamic stabilization produced greater NT-proBNP reduction than enalapril without excess renal dysfunction, hyperkalemia, symptomatic hypotension, or angioedema [21]. Its open-label extension suggested early clinical-event separation when therapy was started before discharge [22]. TRANSITION further supported initiation either in hospital or soon after discharge, emphasizing stabilization, renal function, potassium, and blood pressure as key determinants of success [23].

Reverse remodeling provides another mechanistic bridge between biomarkers and outcomes. In PROVE-HF, reductions in NT-proBNP after sacubitril/valsartan initiation correlated with improvements in left ventricular volumes and ejection fraction [24]. EVALUATE-HF did not show a significant reduction in aortic characteristic impedance versus enalapril, but did show favorable ventricular remodeling measures [25]. In patients with HFrEF and functional mitral regurgitation, sacubitril/valsartan reduced regurgitant volume more than valsartan, suggesting that ventricular unloading and remodeling may improve secondary valve disease [26].

In heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), results are more nuanced. PARAGON-HF narrowly missed statistical significance for its primary composite of total heart-failure hospitalizations and cardiovascular death, but suggested benefit in patients with lower ejection fraction within the preserved range [27]. Women appeared to derive greater reduction in heart-failure hospitalizations than men [28]. Pooled analyses across PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF support a continuum of ARNI responsiveness, with treatment effect greatest at lower ejection fractions and attenuating as ejection fraction rises [29]. These findings underpin contemporary use in HFrEF, selective use in mildly reduced ejection fraction, and individualized consideration in HFpEF.

After acute myocardial infarction complicated by left ventricular dysfunction or pulmonary congestion, PARADISE-MI did not significantly reduce the primary composite compared with ramipril, although event patterns were directionally favorable and safety was acceptable [30]. Thus, sacubitril/valsartan is not a universal replacement for ACE inhibition after infarction, but it remains foundational in chronic symptomatic HFrEF.

In practice, sacubitril/valsartan should replace ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy in eligible HFrEF patients, with a 36-hour washout after ACE inhibitors to reduce angioedema risk. Starting dose should reflect blood pressure, renal function, prior renin-angiotensin system inhibitor dose, age, and congestion status. Monitoring focuses on hypotension, renal function, potassium, and volume status; diuretic reduction is often needed as natriuresis improves. The overall evidence positions ARNI therapy as a mortality-reducing, hospitalization-reducing, remodeling-promoting treatment central to modern HFrEF care, with evolving but more selective roles across the broader ejection-fraction spectrum.
